findings.defect: The reentry still reads as two primitives stuck together. (1) The shock layer from the side is a clipped white D-shaped lens with a smooth outline and a soft lilac halo, glued to the shield (plasma-1.0-night: 96 % of an 80x120 patch at 255). (2) The wake is a parallel-sided translucent pink hose, wider than the capsule, of constant width and constant hue to the frame edge: (214,180,185) at intensity 1.0 and (135,105,121) at 0.3, crossed by ruler-straight streaks. It reads as a plastic tube or a light-saber, not hot gas. (3) From the front the head is a featureless clipped white ellipse with a soft halo; at 0.3 it becomes a white ring around a mottled inner disc, and the far end of the wake is a grey pencil point. (4) From behind it is still the solar-eclipse look: a mauve disc inside a white ring, with hairline straight yellow spokes on one side. (5) The capsule's own back shell is grey and unlit, with dark streaks from the sheath laid over it, rather than glowing orange at the shoulder.
findings.realReference: reentry-chutes/eft1-plasma-side-window.jpg: a pink-magenta to salmon field (mean 120,95,109) of fine, dense, irregular streaks of varied brightness, with a white-yellow core at the window edge and no smooth surfaces. reentry-chutes/progress42-reentry.jpg and dragon-reentry-from-iss.jpg: from afar, a compact point-like clipped head with a thin trail that narrows and dims. Hayabusa and Orion tracking footage: the glow wraps the shoulder and the wake tapers into the trail; there is never a tube of constant width or a ring.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/vfx/plasma.ts: the shock layer is still a thin shell at the standoff distance, scaled up to clip, so it renders as a lens. The wake volume's radius is set by the shoulder and widens slowly (the 2.5x slower widening of this round), so it reads as a cylinder. One colour ramp with wakeGain 0.05 has no temperature gradient along or across the wake. The streak noise is drawn along the axis at a single scale. The near-eye cut still removes the wake for the camera behind. reentry.light.efficacy is too low to light the back shell.
findings.fixDirection: Make the wake narrow from about one shield radius at the shoulder to a fraction of it within a few body lengths. Within the first body lengths, drop its luminance by at least 10x with a hot-to-cool colour ramp (white-yellow, salmon, dull red), and fade its edge with distance from the axis, so the core is brighter than the rim. Replace the single streak field with two or three octaves of streamers that break, kink and vary in brightness (the EFT-1 frames). Give the shock layer a thickness that falls off smoothly ahead of the shield, and let its bloom carry the glare instead of a hard-edged clipped shell. Behind: draw the sheath from inside the wake rather than a disc and ring. Raise the plasma light so the shoulder and back shell take an orange rim.

findings.view: splash/impact-0.1s.png, impact-0.4s.png, impact-1s.png, impact-1.8s.png, impact-2.5s.png, impact-5s.png, close-0.4s.png, close-0.4s-live.png, close-1s.png
findings.defect: The splash still reads as a particle effect. At +0.1 s it is a flat white ellipse with a fur of short radial needles. At +0.4 s and +1 s it is a soft white bowl (close-0.4s: median 223,223,225) inside a snow globe of thousands of identical round white dots of one or two sizes, spread evenly over a flat elliptical annulus. Close up (close-1s) they are a dense sparkle field of uniform discs reaching far beyond the crown, like confetti or snow. There are no sheets, ligaments, fingers or chunky spray of varied size. The capsule is hidden in a white blur. At +1.8 s and +2.5 s the mist is a ring of soft cotton puffs. Afterwards (+5 s) the foam is a flat turquoise disc with scattered white chips and an elliptical outline, and the sea itself never moves.
findings.realReference: sea-surface-close/: Apollo, Orion and Dragon splashdowns throw an irregular, lumpy, translucent wall of white water one to two capsule heights high. It breaks into ragged curtains and spray of very different sizes that falls back within a second or two, then leaves a boiling pale-turquoise patch with foam streaks. heavy-seas-essex-1960.jpg: spray sheets are white and translucent, and old foam is a reticulated lace of filaments, not chips on a disc.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/vfx/splash.ts and particles.ts: tens of thousands of droplets from three ring emitters with an even angular spread and a narrow size range, each widened to at least a pixel and lit to near white. The crown is an axisymmetric sheet whose rim noise of this round (three scales) is too small to break the bowl silhouette. The foam (FOAM_WGSL) is a disc of one analytic radius with thresholded white chips.
findings.fixDirection: Cut the droplet count by an order of magnitude and spread their sizes over at least 20:1 (a few large blobs, many sub-pixel ones drawn as soft energy-conserving smudges). Cluster them into fingers along the crown's tear lines and give them sun glints, not a uniform white. Build the crown from a thickness field that varies strongly in azimuth (fingers, gaps, an asymmetric lean from the horizontal entry speed) and is translucent at the top. Fall the spray back under gravity within 1-2 s. Draw foam as filaments with drift streaks over an aerated tint, with no disc outline, and ask the ocean package for a ring-wave disturbance.

findings.view: explosion/day-0.2s.png, day-0.6s.png, day-1.5s.png, close-0.6s.png, close-0.6s-live.png, night-0.2s.png, night-1.5s.png, close-night-0.6s.png
findings.defect: Between 0.2 s and 1.5 s the fireball reads as a ball of golden glitter crumbs: hundreds of small yellow-beige blobs on a brown haze. After the 0.03 s flash nothing in it clips: the 130x130 patch at 0.2 s has 0.17 % of pixels at 250+ and a median (133,132,141) that is the sky showing through. About eight thick, straight, pale-cream rods of constant width with rounded ends stick out of it (a sea-urchin look). One secondary burst is a square block of bright dots with flat sides (close-0.6s, near x 740, y 345). A vertical column of evenly spaced dots rises from the top. At night the whole ball is one sepia tone, with the same glitter and rods, and it lights nothing but a faint brown glow at the bottom edge. The soot cloud at 3.5 s and 7 s is the best part of the package: dark grey billows with lit and shaded sides.
findings.realReference: Vehicle break-ups (CRS-7, Antares Orb-3, AMOS-6, Starship tests): for the first second the core clips white-yellow; deep orange folds wrap glowing cracks and roll into black soot, with continuous turbulent structure and no granular sparkle. Debris trails are thin, curved, kinked smoke threads with a bright head. liftoff-ascent/artemis1-launch-1.jpg: a night fire lights its own smoke orange (167,128,78) and the ground around it.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/vfx/fireball.ts: the fire emission is a high power of a noise field, so it lights isolated cells (the crumbs) instead of a continuous flame, and its luminance after the flash is held below the exposure white. The secondary bursts use the same noise on a small radius inside a box-shaped bound (item 21). Fragments are trail.ts tubes of fixed radius (fragmentSmoke) with the noise switched off while they glow, hence straight rods. The chips are emitted from one point each step (the dot column, item 26).
findings.fixDirection: Drive the fire with a smooth temperature field (a low power of a turbulent density, not local^7). Keep the core above 5e5 cd/m^2 for the first third of the duration so it clips and blooms. Map the temperature through white, yellow, orange and dull red, with soot extinction rising as the gas cools, so dark folds wrap bright cracks from the start. Spawn secondaries inside the ball and scale their noise frequency with radius, using a bound that follows the radius. Make fragment trails thin (0.2-0.4 m), noisy, widening and gravity-curved, with a bright head. Jitter the chip emission in space and time. At night, make the fireball a sphere light that is strong enough to light the ground.

findings.view: liftoff/t0-night.png, t3-night.png, t10-night.png, liftoff-chase/t0-night.png, t3-night.png, t6-night.png, t6-night-live.png, t10-night.png, liftoff-probe/pad-night-T2.png, pad-night-T6.png
findings.defect: The night lift-off now reads, but not as the real thing. The steam cloud lit by the flame is the same cream white as by day ((222,203,176) at T+10, against (201,169,145) in the day jet), so the frame looks like a daylight cloud cut out of black. The pool of light on the apron is a smooth, uniform radial falloff. 52-68 % of each pad frame is at 4/255 or below. The hull is lit at T+0 but goes dark from T+3, and at T+10 the vehicle above the flame has vanished. Only the jet and the cloud remain, with no rim light, no lit tower and no glow in the sky above the pad. The jet clips (5 % of a 40x220 patch) but carries no glare.
findings.realReference: liftoff-ascent/artemis1-launch-1.jpg: the cloud is lit orange-brown (167,128,78) and grades to dark brown on the side away from the flame; the towers are lit warm, and the plume floods the whole pad with 8 % of pixels clipped. atlasv-oa6-liftoff.jpg: the exhaust cloud is warm (230,201,160), and the tower and vehicle are rimmed. sts97-smoke-steam-night.jpg: smoke is lit only on the plume-facing side, and the rest falls to near black.
findings.likelyCause: Night scattering in src/render/vfx/smoke.ts uses the plume term with the plume's own colour, but without a strong falloff with distance from the flame or the smoke's own shadowing, so the cloud lights evenly. The three ground lights of this round sit on a ring at the foot and light the ground only. Nothing lights the hull once it has climbed above them. The source radius on LocalLight (vfx-5) is still open, so a light near the hull would clip it.
findings.fixDirection: Shade the night cloud from the jet outwards: in-scatter that falls with the square of the distance to the jet segment, and is extinguished by the cloud between the jet and the sample, so the face toward the flame is bright orange and the far side is dark brown. Tint the flame light warmer (about 1800-2200 K). Keep one light on the jet just below the nozzles, so the aft hull keeps an orange rim while the vehicle climbs (with a floor on the distance until vfx-5 lands). Feed the clipped jet into bloom with a wide glare.

findings.view: plumes-close/booster-45m.png, booster-45m-live.png, booster-45m-night.png, booster-110m.png, liftoff-chase/t10-day.png, engine-atlas-9m/sl-full.png, sl-full-live.png, ascent/12km.png, perf-ascent.png
findings.defect: No booster flame clips, by day or by night, and none has glare. In booster-45m the column measures median (245,236,219) with a maximum of 249; booster-45m-night gives (246,237,221), the same picture on black. In engine-atlas-9m/sl-full the flame is (239,216,186) and its core (192,171,162). The jet is a parallel-sided cream-orange column of vertical streaks with rows of soft white dots for the shock cells, and it is stippled even in the live frame. The flat annulus between the bells glows a uniform white, as if it were the source (item 13). At 2 km and 12 km the plume is a soft orange-cream cone, plausible in shape but without a blinding head.
findings.realReference: liftoff-ascent/apollo4-liftoff.jpg: deep yellow-orange F-1 plumes (238,206,136) with a clipped core, about 10x the sky. sts51f-ignition.jpg: SRB plumes are blinding white, with 9.9 % of the frame clipped and the vehicle lit warm. INDEX key number: the plume core is clipped (Y 1.0) in EVERY exposure.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/vfx/plumes.ts clamps rgb to HDR_MAX*0.25 and its emission falls below white at the exposure the scene settles on. The highlight term in exposure.ts still pulls the exposure down to the flame. Bloom gets nothing above its threshold. The shock cells are Gaussian discs.
findings.fixDirection: Make the core and the first one or two vehicle diameters of the jet exceed the exposure white by 2-3 stops at the daylight exposure (check against the sunny-16 EV of the pad scene) and feed bloom so a glare surrounds it. Let the downstream flame break into large eddies at the scale of the jet radius instead of parallel streaks. Draw the cells as oblique diamonds with a bright Mach disc for the first few cells only. Add a spec: in plumes-close/booster-45m at least 2 % of the jet pixels clip.

findings.view: engine-atlas-9m/10km-full.png, 10km-min.png, engine-vela-2v/30km-min.png, engine-lyra-a/30km-min.png, engine-lyra-d/30km-min.png (and their sheets)
findings.defect: New rendering fault at 10 and 30 km: the plume is cut into pieces. Several hundred pixels downstream of the nozzle a second, detached plume segment starts with a hard, straight edge across the jet axis, with a gap of darker sky between it and the first segment. In engine-atlas-9m/10km-full and 10km-min a hard horizontal seam also runs through the plume exactly along the horizon line, so the part over the ground and the part over the sky have different brightness and texture.
findings.realReference: liftoff-ascent/apollo6-f1-trail.jpg and falcon9-twilight-plume.jpg: a plume and its trail form one continuous body, widening smoothly from the nozzle with no gaps or straight cuts, and the background behind them does not change them.
findings.likelyCause: Hypothesis 1: the exhaust trail (trail.ts) is fed from a node min(length/2, 30 re) behind the nozzles and begins with a flat cap, while the plume volume fades out at its window before reaching it; at 10-30 km both are visible separately. Hypothesis 2 (the seam): the half-resolution march or the depth-aware upsample treats ground and sky pixels differently (the per-sample applyAtmosphere distance, or the depth test against scene.depthHalf at the horizon), so the composite changes across the horizon edge.
findings.fixDirection: Switch trails off in the lab to identify the detached segment. Then overlap the plume's far fade and the trail's near fade along the same axis and radius, and round or fade the trail cap. For the seam, compare a frame with the horizon below the plume, and make the per-sample atmosphere and the upsample independent of whether the background is ground or sky. Add a spec: the plume's luminance along the axis has no step larger than about 20 % between neighbouring samples.

findings.view: plumes-close/staging-separation-70m.png, staging-retro-70m.png, staging/2.56s-separation.png, staging/2.9s-retro.png, staging/3.6s-coast.png, vacuum-ignition/ignition-0.05s.png, ignition-0.3s.png
findings.defect: Staging and vacuum ignition read as sprites. At separation, four soft cream cones fan out of the interstage like searchlight beams, with a grainy stippled fringe where they cross the hull edge. Around them is a spray of small gold rectangles (rectangular confetti, 3x crop of staging-separation-70m). The retro firing adds clumps of identical white dots, and at coast the gap is ringed by dots of one size. Vacuum ignition at 0.05 s is an orange sunburst: straight radial rays fanning out from a point above the stage, with a dithered, speckled outline, larger than the stage and lighting nothing.
findings.realReference: liftoff-ascent/falcon9-first-stage-separation.jpg: after staging the upper stage is a compact orange-white point with an expanding glow, and the first stage's exhaust a faint wisp. Saturn V S-IC/S-II staging film: eight retro jets as short bright streaks, then a brief, thin, fast, translucent gas cloud gone within half a second.
findings.likelyCause: The separation gas and ignition flash are drawn as cones and a fan with radial noise from plumes.ts (plume.solid at vacuum pressure for the retro and ullage motors). The gold rectangles and white dots are particles.ts sparks and chips with sub-pixel sizes widened to one pixel (item 22), drawn without motion stretch. The radial rays come from noise stretched along the radial direction from the nozzle.
findings.fixDirection: Make the separation gas a short-lived expanding translucent shell (gone in 0.3-0.5 s), not cones. Give the retro jets a short bright core and thin smoke. Replace the confetti with a few debris pieces of very different sizes, stretched by their motion during the exposure. For ignition, use an expanding puff whose noise is isotropic, not radial, so it has no god-rays, and blur its rim instead of dithering it.

findings.view: liftoff/t3-day.png, t10-day.png, liftoff-chase/t3-day.png, t6-day.png, t6-day-live.png, t10-day.png, inside-cloud-t6-day.png, inside-cloud-t6-night.png, perf-lift-off-from-a-chase-camera-at-150-m.png, perf-lift-off-worst-case.png, perf-lift-off-from-inside-the-cloud.png
findings.defect: The pad cloud has better cauliflower billows than before and the hairlines are gone, but four problems remain. (1) At T+10 it is still a low mound, less than a third of the vehicle's height, and soft everywhere. (2) It is a warm cream (about 222,210,190) with no tan exhaust and no brilliant white steam. (3) In the live T+6 frame, dark wormy dendritic holes and a stippled dither fringe sit in its right half. (4) The flame enters it as a cream column, and the 'ice' dots above the trench are identical round white discs. From inside the cloud the frame is one flat orange-tan fill with the mount as a ghost (item 27).
findings.realReference: liftoff-ascent/artemis2-launch-2.jpg: brilliant white steam spreading low and wide from the trench, the dominant feature of the frame, with crisp towers. apollo4-liftoff.jpg: a huge tan exhaust cloud with brown shadow sides (144,113,101) billowing sideways. sts134-ssme-ignition.jpg: a towering white steam cloud with hard curled edges.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/vfx/smoke.ts: the erosion is still a steep threshold that cuts holes to zero density (the dark worms over the shadowed ground). The fringe is resolved at quarter resolution. Single scattering with the plume colour tints everything cream. padSmoke yield and buoyancy keep the cloud low.
findings.fixDirection: Raise the steam yield and the trench-jet momentum so the cloud reaches several hundred metres by T+10. Separate steam (white, high albedo) from exhaust (tan), and add a multiple-scattering ambient term so gaps read as grey cloud. Replace the threshold erosion with a soft remap that keeps a density floor. Resolve the fringe at half resolution. Inside the cloud, keep a gradient towards the jet.

findings.view: engine-solids/sl-les.png, sl-les-live.png, sl-les-close-live.png, sl-retro.png, 10km-les.png, 10km-retro.png, 30km-les.png, 30km-retro.png, 60km-les.png, vac-les.png, vac-retro.png
findings.defect: The solid motors now have a white-hot root, but the plume beyond it is a soft cream cone that looks out of focus, with no billows, no lit and shaded sides and no ragged edge. The four retro motors are soft cream fingers. At 30 km, 60 km and in vacuum the cones turn into grainy, stippled spotlight beams with straight edges.
findings.realReference: liftoff-ascent/sts51f-ignition.jpg: SRB plumes are blinding white with hard edges, turning into dense white-grey smoke with lumpy cauliflower edges. Pad Abort 1 and Ascent Abort 2 footage: a long clipped flame, then billowing smoke with a strong lit/shaded contrast.
findings.likelyCause: plumes.ts jetSample: the smoke boundary is the analytic cone displaced by a few per cent, with a single constant sun term and no shadowing, so it reads as a soft cone. At low pressure the halo is sparse and the half-resolution jitter shows through as stipple.
findings.fixDirection: Displace the smoke boundary with billows that scale with the local jet radius, growing downstream. Add a two- or three-step shadow toward the sun. At low pressure, fade the stippled halo and widen the fan smoothly, as in the vacuum plumes of this round.

findings.view: chutes/mains-full-frontlit.png, mains-full-backlit.png, mains-reef1-backlit.png, mains-reef2-backlit.png, drogues-full.png, drogues-reefed.png, splash/before.png
findings.defect: The canopy fabric reads as a quilted tile pattern. Every gore is broken into boxy panels separated by dark seams, a high-contrast grid of orange and white bricks with self-shadowed lumps on each panel. From the drogue distance it breaks into orange-white noise. Against the light the canopies are opaque and dull, and do not glow. The reefed mains are closed tiled tubes and spheres (items 18 and 19), and the clusters interpenetrate.
findings.realReference: reentry-chutes/artemis2-mains.jpg: the gores read as smooth red and white stripes; the panel grid is a faint fine texture, with a few white 'window' squares, and the canopy is a smooth dome with a crisp hem. soyuz-ms17-chute.jpg: a sunlit canopy is smooth and bright (224,185,161).
findings.likelyCause: src/render/vfx/chutes.ts: the panel pattern is drawn with dark seam lines at a contrast close to the gore stripes, plus a normal or shading bump per panel. The pattern is not filtered with distance (item 25). The lantern term is scaled down at low inflation.
findings.fixDirection: Make the seams a subtle albedo variation (a few per cent), not dark gaps, and drop the per-panel bulge. Keep the stripes as the dominant pattern. Filter the pattern with screen-space derivatives. Keep single-layer translucency at full strength when the canopy is backlit.

findings.defect: After cut-away the canopies no longer stand as domes, but they become curled tiled sausages (a question-mark shape in cut-away-6s and the perf picture). Their suspension lines hang below them as bundles of rigid, perfectly straight vertical rods of equal length. A second after release they look like jellyfish tentacles; later they look like rain falling past the capsule. In impact-5s, bundles of straight vertical line segments enter from the top of the frame with no canopy attached.
findings.realReference: Orion, Apollo and Dragon recovery footage: the released lines go slack at once and trail behind the collapsing canopy in loose curves; the cloth streams and folds and settles on the water as a sheet. sea-surface-close/apollo9-floats.jpg: spent canopies lie flat on the water, bright and saturated.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/vfx/chutes.ts drift: each line is a straight segment hanging under gravity from its gore, without sag or a free end that trails the canopy's motion. The collapse bends the profile along one axis into a tube.
findings.fixDirection: Draw each released line as a curve (a catenary or a short chain of segments) trailing the canopy with drag, with random lengths and a shared confluence that stays attached. Collapse the canopy into a streaming, crumpled shape that falls skirt-first, then lies flat on the water.

findings.defect: Lunar dust is still painted on the ground. At 30 m it is a faint fan of soft spokes running towards the camera, with no height. At 10 m and 5 m it is a slight brightening of the regolith with a few streak particles. The horizon stays razor sharp and nothing is veiled, so there is no sheet streaming outward. By night, at 30 m, the plume is an opaque white lampshade cone, the legs clip to white lines with one strut dotted, and at 3 m the ground is a glowing white pool with scattered dashes (item 23).
findings.realReference: Apollo 11 to 17 descent film from the LM window, Blue Ghost and Chang'e landing video: a thin, bright, fast sheet streams radially along the surface and washes out the rocks and craters under it, so the horizon below about 10 m softens; fine streaks flicker inside the sheet, and the lander's shadow falls on it. moon-surface/: regolith is neutral grey, and shadows near bright ground are filled.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/vfx/dust.ts: the sheet's optical depth and height are too small to occlude anything, and the streak field is still angular noise with little radial variation. The night plume (plume.methalox-lander) keeps a bright near field in vacuum.
findings.fixDirection: Give the sheet an optical depth of 1-2 at the impingement ring, falling as r0/r, and a height that grows as the lander descends, so the ground and horizon are veiled below 10 m. Add forward scattering towards a low sun. Lower the lander's vacuum near-field luminance and hold its hue when it clips.

findings.defect: New: a hairline, ruler-straight orange line starts just ahead of the shock layer and runs forward and down past the capsule to the right frame edge, about 1 px wide and of constant brightness (3x crop of plasma-0.3-night, x 900-1280, y 540-640). It is in all four plasma pictures, day and night, and a similar faint line crosses the upper left of front-1.0-live. Nothing real lies ahead of a reentering capsule.
findings.realReference: reentry-chutes/progress42-reentry.jpg and dragon-reentry-from-iss.jpg: the only luminous feature is the head and the trail behind it.
findings.likelyCause: Hypothesis: an exhaust or reentry trail ribbon (trail.ts) keeps a stale node from where the lab first placed the vessel or from before an origin rebase, and the sub-pixel widening draws the segment from that node to the current head; or a debris or fragment trail left over from the scene start. Not confirmed.
findings.fixDirection: Switch trails, particles and fragments off one at a time in the reentry lab to find the source. Reset a trail when its vessel teleports or the floating origin rebases, and never draw a segment longer than speed x frame time x a small factor.

findings.defect: From 50 km at night the reentry trail is still a ruler-straight salmon line of constant width (about 4 px) and constant brightness, from the head to the left frame edge. It has no fade, no taper, no beading and no colour change along its length. By day the trail behind the head is a faint dark-brown line, so the two regimes look unrelated. The head itself is a clipped white teardrop with glare, which is an improvement.
findings.realReference: reentry-chutes/progress42-reentry.jpg: a short orange-white streak with a brighter leading head and a dimmer, slightly wavy tail that fades out. dragon-reentry-from-iss.jpg: a thin streak with a compact bright head and a slowly fading tail.
findings.likelyCause: src/render/vfx/trail.ts: reentry.trail lifetime 18 s with a single glow term at constant luminance; at sub-pixel width the tube is widened to a fixed width, and the noise is invisible at that width.
findings.fixDirection: Split the glow into a hot term that e-folds over 0.3-0.6 s and a faint train, so the line dims by orders of magnitude across the frame. Grade its colour from white through orange to dull red with age, and modulate brightness along the length at a 0.5-2 km scale.

findings.view: rcs/pulse-sun.png, all-sun.png, all-sun-12m.png, all-sun-12m-live.png, pulse-shadow.png, all-shadow.png, all-shadow-12m.png, all-shadow-12m-live.png
findings.defect: The long grey light shafts are gone, but now the firings barely show. In sunlight each thruster is a tiny soft glow at the nozzle that a player would not notice. In shadow the only sign is a small lit arc on the hull rim, while the puff itself and the rest of the hull stay black.
findings.realReference: Shuttle and Dragon thruster firings: a sharp, bright flash at the nozzle and a short, wide translucent puff visible for a fraction of a second. At night the primary thrusters light the nearby structure brilliantly in orange-white.
findings.likelyCause: plumes.json plume.rcs: the halo, length and luminance were cut so far that the puff falls below the exposure, and the light efficacy is low.
findings.fixDirection: Keep the wide, short cone, but give it a bright nozzle flash (5e4 cd/m^2 or more over a few exit diameters) and a puff that scatters sunlight at a visible level for 1-2 m. Raise the light so the hull around a firing thruster is clearly lit in shadow, and make the pulse envelope sharp.

findings.defect: The soot phase still has fake details. Cool white specks are scattered over the dark smoke like stars. Some pits in the cloud are near black (day-3.5s: a 50x50 patch at median 49,47,48) with hard edges. A short dark vertical bar still crosses the left fragment trail in close-2.5s (4x crop at x 290-305, y 140-190). From 1.5 s, the thick straight rods hang outside the cloud with flat ends.
findings.realReference: Explosion smoke in footage is continuous and soft-shadowed. Debris and embers glow orange and fade, they are not white specks, and fragment trails are thin threads.
findings.likelyCause: The chips (particles.ts) are lit white and kept at one pixel. The pits come from the extinction field's erosion over the dark interior. The dark bar is unexplained (item 26).
findings.fixDirection: Make the chips glowing embers that cool and fade, or dark tumbling pieces lit by the sun. Soften the erosion floor in the soot. Find the bar by switching off debris, trails and fragments one at a time.

findings.defect: Half-resolution grain is still visible. Where volumes cross a hull edge, a band of sandy stipple runs along the silhouette (the separation crop). The sea-level booster core is speckled in the live frame. The low-pressure solid cones, the ignition rim and the cloud fringe are dithered rather than smooth.
findings.realReference: Gas, smoke and dust are smooth at pixel scale in every frame of a photograph.
findings.likelyCause: One blue-noise sample per half-resolution pixel on a short march, with the depth-aware upsample doing no spatial filtering (items 20 and 24). The live frames still show it, so temporal filtering does not remove it everywhere.
findings.fixDirection: Add a small depth-aware spatial filter on the half-resolution volume image before the composite, and reject far volume samples behind a near hull edge.

findings.defect: The canopies cast hard, near-black blobs on the sunlit sea ((2,14,39) against a sea of (13,53,106)), with a stippled edge.
findings.realReference: sea-surface-close/: under a clear sky the sea in shadow still reflects the sky and is only moderately darker than the sea beside it, with a soft edge.
findings.likelyCause: The shadow of the canopy caster removes all of the sea's lighting, including the sky reflection; the ocean or core shading treats the shadow as a full occluder of the specular sky term (item 28).
findings.fixDirection: Check on the real ocean with live filtering. If it persists, file it to the ocean package or core-support with this picture: the shadow should affect only the sun term.

findings.defect: The functional exposure spec fails: a 0.415 EV step between the frame before impact and the first in the water, against a 0.4 limit. The matrix pictures cannot show it: the lab holds the splash camera at the exposure of a real sea, so the sky is the same (147,161,180) in all seven splash frames, while the meter left to itself moves.
findings.realReference: Recovery footage: the exposure does not react to the capsule going under; the white water clips.
findings.likelyCause: The meter loses the white capsule hull as it submerges (the fixer's reading), and the white water does not replace it in the 99th percentile.
findings.fixDirection: Have core-support bound the highlight term by day (the item-1 request), or take the matrix splash frames with the meter free, so the pictures show what a player sees.
